clue.text: When he treats roots, don't hit out!

definitions.text: When he treats roots, don't hit out!

indicators.note: out here means put out of order, so the letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning to a patient not to lash out while a dentist works on their tooth roots.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal 'out' rearranges ROOTS, DONT and HIT (twelve letters), and the whole clue also describes the specialist who works on teeth and their roots.
explanation.definitionFit: A dental specialist straightens and treats teeth, working down to the roots of a patient's mouth.

clue.text: One who resists problem at work

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work
a poser is a puzzling problem

explanation.surface: A resister causing trouble at work.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stands against something is an adversary or objector.

indicators.note: by ear means the word is heard, not spelt

parts.note: instructed means taught

explanation.surface: A nervous pupil learning music by ear.
explanation.definitionFit: A tightly stretched, strained thing is tense.

clue.text: Card-game? Here is one, on the shelf

definitions.meaning: a children's card game where the player left with the unmatched queen loses

definitions.text: Here is one, on the shelf
definitions.meaning: a woman past the age thought likely to marry, said to be on the shelf

explanation.surface: Someone pointing out a card game sitting on a shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the shelf' is an old idiom for an unmarried woman passed over; the clue's dated phrase is the setter's.
explanation.definitionFit: The card game is named after an unwed older woman, the dated sense of being left on the shelf.

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
to deal is to share out, as cards

explanation.surface: Assay tests checking gold shares.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tests of gold' suggests assaying, but 'of' only joins; OR is the heraldic word for gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe trials and hard experiences test a person's endurance.

definitions.meaning: a drop of water rolling down someone's cheek when crying
a rent is a rip in cloth

explanation.surface: An impudent fall in what tenants pay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheeky' looks like insolent, but it means on the cheek; 'rent' is the noun for a rip.
explanation.definitionFit: A weeping drop runs down the cheek, and a rip in fabric is a rent.

parts.note: usage is custom or habit

explanation.surface: A custom-made car from South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banger' is British slang for both an old car and a sausage; here it is the food.
explanation.definitionFit: A banger is the British slang for a pork link, fried and served with mash.

clue.text: Arrogant, demanding Platform Ten is made ready

indicators.note: made ready means put into a fresh order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An arrogant traveller insisting Platform Ten be prepared for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone conceited has an inflated sense of their own significance.

parts.note: pop is a word for dad, so idols who are pops are paternal role models

explanation.surface: A question about music stars.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop idols' suggests music stars, but 'pop' is a dad.
explanation.definitionFit: Men looked up to as paternal role models are idolised as dads.

parts.note: ex- is a prefix meaning former
Ezra Pound was an American modernist poet

explanation.surface: A request to explain the work of an American poet from the past.
explanation.definitionFit: To interpret something is to set out and explain its meaning in detail.

parts.note: a medical-sounding phrase about a worrying blood test, reread as a frightening nobleman with a taste for blood

explanation.surface: A doctor reporting a worrying result from a blood test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blood-count' is not a test: it is a Count obsessed with blood, the vampire of Bram Stoker's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Stoker's vampire is a Transylvanian Count who terrifies people and drinks their blood.

clue.text: Duke, say, holding maximum number of Western dollars?

definitions.text: Duke, say, holding maximum number of Western dollars?

parts.words: Duke, say, holding maximum number of Western dollars
parts.note: dukes is slang for hands closed for a fight, and the Western film title speaks of a handful of dollars, the most a closed hand holds

explanation.surface: An aristocrat in a cowboy film grabbing as much money as he can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duke' is slang for a clenched hand (from rhyming slang 'Duke of York' = fork, an old word for hand), and 'A Fistful of Dollars' is a Western film.
explanation.definitionFit: A clenched hand, called a duke in boxing slang, holds a fistful of whatever it grasps.

indicators.note: in tells us the chemical symbol goes inside the state abbreviation

parts.note: Na is the chemical symbol for sodium

explanation.surface: A chemistry note that sodium in California has been reduced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a verb describing the sodium, but it is the definition: a cut is an old British word for an artificial waterway.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a man-made waterway dug for boats was called a cut, as it was cut through the land.

definitions.meaning: a tub fitted in a house's washroom
a spa city in Somerset, England

explanation.surface: A football match played at home for a team called City.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixture' suggests a sports match, but here it is a fitting in a home; Bath is a Roman spa city in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: A tub for washing is fitted in a house, and the Somerset spa town shares the same name.

parts.note: Aden is a port in Yemen

explanation.surface: A ship leaving port fully loaded.
explanation.definitionFit: A loaded ship carries a full burden, weighed down with goods.

clue.text: He will shortly ring — to say this?

parts.note: he will, contracted, is he'll
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: Someone will phone soon and needs a greeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' looks like a phone call, but it is the letter O; the word is what you say when answering.
explanation.definitionFit: A greeting word is what someone says on picking up a call.

indicators.note: switch means swap around, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lighting control used on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dimmer-switch' looks like stage lighting, but 'switch' rearranges A DIMMER; the Mermaid is a London theatre at Blackfriars.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mermaid is a playhouse on the Thames in the City of London, named after an old tavern.

indicators.note: drunk means tipsy and muddled, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: A woman called Ursula has had a beer or two.
explanation.walkthrough: The name Ursula comes from Latin for 'little female bear', so a name defines the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The name derives from Latin ursa, a female ursine animal, so it means a little one of those.

definitions.meaning: people who keep quiet and closed up, like a shellfish
natives is a trade name for British-farmed shellfish of this kind

explanation.surface: Quiet people described as local inhabitants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Natives' are oysters raised in British beds, such as Whitstable natives; a tight-lipped person is said to be as close as one.
explanation.definitionFit: Shut-mouthed people are likened to shellfish that stay clamped closed, and native is a name for farmed British ones.

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: A broken promise made by a part-time worker.
explanation.definitionFit: A player paid for sport but not full-time is half professional.

clue.text: Low seat that is for a police informer

parts.note: a stool is a low seat
ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: An informer sitting on a low seat.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang a stool pigeon tips off the police.

parts.note: a cell is a small cramped room, a hole
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A sculptor scoring a hole-in-one at golf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hole-in-one' looks like golf, but it is three pieces; Benvenuto Cellini was an Italian Renaissance sculptor and goldsmith.
explanation.definitionFit: Benvenuto Cellini was a Renaissance Florentine metalworker who made the bronze Perseus statue.

indicators.note: gone bust means broken, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A watch company has gone bankrupt.
explanation.definitionFit: The Choctaw are a Native American people of the south-eastern United States.

definitions.meaning: his Symphony No 4 is named after the country he toured
sweet vermouth is called It, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: Mendelssohn's fourth drink of vermouth.
explanation.walkthrough: Mendelssohn's Fourth Symphony has a national name; red vermouth is called It in a gin and It.
explanation.definitionFit: The symphony is named for the land it celebrates, and sweet vermouth comes from that country.

parts.note: to can mean towards, approaching
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's qualification

explanation.surface: A doctor approaching a patient realises the situation is serious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grave' looks like an adjective meaning serious, but it is the noun: a burial place.
explanation.definitionFit: A burial place or vault where a body is laid is a grave.

definitions.note: plural, though the answer is one punctuation mark; colons are stops in punctuation

indicators.note: most of means drop the final letter of the word

parts.note: a colony is a settlement abroad

explanation.surface: Someone halts most of a village.
explanation.definitionFit: A colon is a punctuation mark, and such marks are traditionally called stops.

indicators.note: central means the middle four letters of the long word

explanation.surface: Something frowned upon in a police force in the middle of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Central Constabulary' sounds like a police force, but 'Central' picks the middle four letters of Constabulary.
explanation.definitionFit: A forbidden thing, in the older spelling, is something society bans and frowns upon.

definitions.meaning: a length of cord or twine

explanation.surface: A group of musicians playing stringed instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: A cord is a length of thread, and a long strip or stripe is also a band.

definitions.meaning: to catch on is to understand
a slender shoot of a tree

explanation.surface: Something snagging on a small branch.
explanation.definitionFit: Grasping a point is catching on, and a slender shoot of a tree is the same word.

clue.text: Well versed in New Latin in respect of marriage

indicators.note: in tells us the short word goes inside the rearranged letters
new means made afresh, so the letters of the language name are rearranged

parts.note: to be up on something is to be well versed in it

explanation.surface: Someone well versed in modern Latin talking about marriage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Latin' looks like a phrase, but 'New' rearranges LATIN to NTIAL, and UP goes inside after the N.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to a wedding or matrimony.

indicators.note: say tells us the words are spoken and heard, not spelt

parts.note: to toe the line is to conform

explanation.surface: Someone pulled a rope to make things fit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toe the line' means to conform; said aloud TOE LINE sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rope by which a vehicle or boat is hauled along is a hawser for towing.

parts.note: an insured thing is covered by a policy
a truck is a wagon

explanation.surface: An insured goods wagon coupled to a railway train.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'train' is not a railway: it is a wagon train of the American West, made up of canvas-topped wagons.
explanation.definitionFit: Pioneer wagon trains in the American West were made up of canvas-topped carts.
